tagline.text: A stretch of white sand near Manila, where mountains meet the sea

children.text: A stretch of white sand beach running for several kilometers along Tayabas Bay in San Juan, at the southeastern tip of Batangas. It's about 3–4 hours from Manila by car, and everything from simple cottages to infinity-pool resorts lines the shore, making it a popular weekend beach getaway.

Laiya is a coastal beach area in the city of San Juan in southeastern Batangas province, spanning the villages of Laiya Aplaya and Laiya Ibabao and the neighboring Hugom area. It faces Tayabas Bay to the south, while the green ridges of the Lobo–San Juan mountain range descend nearly to the shore behind it, giving the area its signature look of white sand and mountains sharing a single view. At about
from Manila, a
3–4-hour
drive, it's beloved by people in the capital region as "a white-sand beach you can reach without flying."

The sand is a white-to-cream mix of finely broken shells and coral — not as powder-soft as Boracay's, but pleasant to walk on barefoot, with clear water. Most of the shoreline is divided into sections run by resorts, and since the sand texture, slope, and rocky patches vary slightly resort by resort, which resort you pick shapes your whole trip.

Once a quiet fishing village, Laiya has grown into a favorite weekend getaway for people from the capital region as beach resorts opened one after another. Options now range from family-friendly cottage resorts to quirky stays like camper-van rooms and capsule-style lodging, up to upscale resorts with infinity pools. In the morning, fishermen hand over their overnight catch to the resorts, and the sunrise over the sea at dawn is one of Laiya's quiet claims to fame.

This is a beach for relaxing and swimming at an easy pace, rather than island hopping or diving. It suits families with children, company workshops and friend groups, and expats who don't want to travel far for a short holiday. For a more active trip, add a hike up nearby Mount Daguldol or a beach-hopping boat tour.

blocks.title: Swim at the white sand beach

children.text: In the dry season, Laiya's waters are calm and clear, good for playing in the water with children. The shallow water in front of the resorts is mostly sandy-bottomed, but rocks and bits of coral appear here and there, so bring aqua shoes.
Laiya faces the sea to the southeast, so the sun rises right out of the water. Head to the beach around
to see the horizon turn red and the silhouettes of fishing boats.
Rent a banca to tour hidden coves, rocky shorelines, and snorkeling spots along the coast. A boat costs about
, so it's affordable if you split it among a group.
A coastal mountain rising
above sea level, starting from Hugom village, about
3–4 hours
to the summit. The popular route passes through forest trails and grassy ridges, overlooks Tayabas Bay and the beach, then finishes with a swim in the sea after coming down.
The larger resorts rent out banana boats, jet skis, kayaks, and stand-up paddleboards. Rates vary by resort and time, so check before you book.

blocks.title: A night in a quirky stay

children.text: A trailer parked right on the beach, round capsule-style rooms, resorts with infinity pools that seem to merge with the sea — at Laiya, the lodging itself becomes part of the fun.
Buying fish, squid, and shrimp that fishermen bring to the beach in the morning, then grilling it yourself at the resort, is a quintessential Laiya pleasure. Some resorts will even cook it for you.

The best time is the
November–May
dry season.
January–February
in particular has good sun without excessive heat and fewer crowds, making it easy to pick a place to stay. During the
March–May
summer break and Holy Week, the sea is calmest and clearest, but resort rates rise and the beach gets crowded on weekends. Midday temperatures run around
June–October

is the rainy season, affected by the southwest monsoon and typhoons; since Laiya's beach opens to the south, waves often pick up and the water turns cloudy on many days. On the plus side, resort rates drop significantly, and some travelers look for off-season deals. When there's a typhoon warning, beachfront resorts ban swimming, and mountain roads can see landslides, so check the PAGASA forecast.

Laiya's accommodations are strung out along the beach, most of them resorts with their own stretch of shoreline. Simple family-style resorts that rent out cottages or tent sites run about
per night; mid-range resorts with air-conditioned rooms and a pool run about
; and upscale resorts with infinity pools and view rooms cost

or more. Long-running La Luz Beach Resort and Laiya Coco Grove, along with Acuatico Beach Resort, known for its infinity pool, are well-known options. Book weeks ahead for weekends and peak season, and note that some resorts don't accept day-tour guests, so check in advance.

Aside from resort restaurants, there aren't many standalone eateries, so people in Laiya often buy seafood and meat and grill it themselves. Buying fish and squid brought in on the beach in the morning, or shopping at the San Juan town public market, keeps costs down. Be sure to try Batangas specialties too: bulalo, a beef bone-marrow soup; Batangas lomi, thick noodles in a rich broth; sinaing na tulingan, tuna slow-cooked in a clay pot; and strong, bitter kapeng barako coffee. These are easy to find in Rosario and Lipa, on the way to and from San Juan town.
Beach conditions vary a great deal from resort to resort in Laiya. Before booking, check recent review photos for sand texture, rocks, and seaweed.
Friday afternoon departures hit heavy traffic on SLEX and around Lipa. Leaving Thursday night or early Saturday morning cuts travel time significantly.
Many resorts charge corkage if you bring in outside food. If you're planning a barbecue, ask about the corkage policy and grill rental fee first.
There are almost no ATMs along Laiya's beachfront. Withdraw enough cash in San Juan town before heading out.
Mobile data is weak at some resorts. If you need to stay reachable for work, check on Wi-Fi availability in advance.
The grassy stretch of Mount Daguldol gets very hot at midday. Start around
5–6 AM
, and register with a local guide at the Hugom trailhead before climbing.
If you're traveling with a group during the summer peak season, claim a beachfront cottage early in the morning to secure a shaded spot.
You can check the list of registered resorts and transport information on the
San Juan tourism website
. The environmental fee of about
per person is paid at the San Juan tourism office or when you arrive at your resort.

There are stretches of Laiya's beach that drop off quickly once you're in the water, and most resorts have no lifeguard on duty. Always have children wear a life vest, and don't swim on days with high waves or a red flag flying.
It's easy to cut your feet on rocks and bits of coral in the shallows. Wear aqua shoes and watch out for sea urchins.
The sun is very strong even in the dry season. Bring reef-safe sunscreen and a rash guard, and rest in the shade at midday.
Jellyfish appear at certain times of year. If stung, rinse with vinegar, and go to a hospital in San Juan town if symptoms are severe.
The road between San Juan and Laiya winds through the mountains and has few streetlights at night. Drive while it's still light out whenever possible.
During the rainy season and typhoon season, check your resort's cancellation and rebooking policy in advance.
